feedback: If a child stops the trace at the immediate food (e.g. 'from the meat'), prompt at each link: 'and where did THAT organism get its energy?' until they reach the Sun.
If a child says the plant's energy comes from the soil, clarify: plants make food using light energy; soil supplies minerals and water, not the energy itself.

If a child treats a meat-eater as disconnected from plants or the Sun, point out the carnivore depends on the plants (or algae) its prey ate, and the whole chain is powered by the Sun through those producers.

If a child treats the food substance itself as the energy, clarify that the energy is what the food carries, not the food material (the matter) — matter can cycle, but the energy is passed along and spent.

If a child thinks the Sun gives an animal its food energy directly, clarify that sunlight can warm an animal's skin (as when a lizard basks), but the energy in its food, which it uses for repair, growth, movement and making its own body heat, reaches it indirectly, through the plants and prey it eats.
Reinforce the one-way arrow: energy streams in from the Sun and is spent on repair/growth/movement/warmth, so it is not cycled back.
activities.intendedInsight: In food chains like these, the energy in an animal's food can be traced link by link back to sunlight captured by a plant or alga; energy flows one way from the Sun and is spent (largely as heat), not recycled around the chain like matter.
learnerActions: Assemble a food chain by placing organisms in order, e.g. Sun → grass → rabbit → fox (and later a different chain such as Sun → algae → fish → seal).

Choose the top animal eating its meal, then trace the energy's source BACKWARDS down the chain (the energy itself flowed forwards, from the Sun to the animal): from the food, back to the organism that ate the plant, back to the plant that captured sunlight, all the way to the Sun.
State in your own words where the energy in that meal originally came from.
Route the arriving food energy into what a body spends it on by sorting it into repair, growth, movement, and keeping warm.
Rebuild with a different chain and check that the trace-back always ends at the Sun.
activities.title: Build and run a trace-the-energy-to-the-Sun model

feedback: For the choice task, if 'animals make their own energy' is selected, re-run the trace: animals get energy from food, which traces back through plants to the Sun.
Mark ordering correct only when the Sun is the starting link.
activities.intendedInsight: The energy in everyday food traces back to the Sun, and that energy is spent on specific body functions.
learnerActions: Put the links of an energy chain in order starting from the Sun.
Match each energy use (repair, growth, movement, warmth) to an everyday example.
Choose where the energy in a fox's food originally came from, rejecting the tempting 'animals make their own energy' option.
activities.title: Order, match, and choose to consolidate the trace-back

feedback: If the chart stops at the food, ask 'and where did that come from?' at each link until it reaches the Sun.
Check the arrow points one way from the Sun and is not drawn as a loop back.
activities.intendedInsight: The same trace-back applies to real meals: the energy in your lunch was once sunlight, and your body spends it on repair, growth, movement, and warmth.
learnerActions: Draw a flow chart of something you ate today, tracing it back through each organism to the Sun.
Label the plant that captured the sunlight and draw a one-way energy arrow from the Sun along the chain.
Write one sentence saying what your body will use that food energy for.
activities.title: Trace your own lunch to the Sun on paper

feedback: When a learner stalls at the food, prompt again for the previous link.
If a learner names the soil as the grass's energy source, clarify soil gives minerals and water, while light gives the energy.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeatedly asking 'and before that?' exposes that, for everyday meals, every link's energy ultimately comes from the Sun through plants or algae.
learnerActions: Take a meal and, with a questioning partner or scientist persona, answer 'and where did that energy come from?' at each link until you reach the Sun.
Explain why the chain stops at the Sun and not earlier.
Explain why the grass's energy comes from sunlight rather than the soil.
activities.title: Socratic 'and before that?' trace-back with a scientist
